project.title: Environment Drives the Succession and Transmission of the Antibiotic Resistome in the Broiler Chicken Gut (PRJCA048852)
project.description: The intensive use of antibiotics in livestock farming has established farms as critical reservoirs for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet the dynamics of ARG transmission between the animal gut and the farm environment remain inadequately characterized. In this longitudinal study, we investigated the succession of the gut resistome in broiler chickens and its interaction with the farm environment, with a focus on horizontal gene transfer. Metagenomic sequencing, high-throughput quantitative PCR, and bacterial isolation were applied to samples from chicken intestines, bedding, and drinking water collected at three key growth stages (0, 7, and 30 days) on a commercial broiler farm. Our results revealed substantial age-dependent restructuring of the gut microbiota and resistome. Although total ARG abundance in chicken feces decreased over time, we observed a significant enrichment of high-risk ARGs. Microbial source tracking identified bedding as the primary source of ARGs in 7- and 30-day-old chickens, confirming environmental acquisition. Strain-level analysis and metagenome-assembled genomes indicated shared bacterial hosts between chickens and their environment. Crucially, plasmid analysis provided direct evidence of horizontal gene transfer, with identical ARG-harboring plasmids isolated simultaneously from chicken intestines and bedding. Risk assessment further showed an increased proportion of high-risk ARGs following environmental exposure. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the farm environment, particularly bedding, acts as both a reservoir and a melting pot for ARGs, driving gut resistome succession through plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer. These results underscore the necessity of targeting environmental management, especially bedding sanitation, to mitigate ARG dissemination in livestock production systems.
